parsed.attack: The evidence offered - a private tracker that went stale [243] and a birthday calendar used once a year [236] - is evidence that one person will not sustain this, and the idea answers it by requiring three people to sustain it. Nobody in that evidence asked for a visible record of who rang Mum, and the reason no authoritative record exists is not that it was hard to build: an explicit scoreboard of filial duty reads as an accusation, which is precisely why families keep this ambiguous. The sibling motivated to install is the over-functioning one, and what they want is for the other two to do more; a ledger does not produce that, it only documents it, which is the version of the truth they are least willing to publish.
parsed.strongest_defence: Families under real caregiving load already build these rotas by hand in group chats and shared calendars, so the coordination behaviour exists and is observed rather than hypothesised; the product is not introducing scorekeeping, it is replacing arithmetic people already do on raw message history, and the ten-second entry is one the caller wants to make because it discharges their turn.
parsed.verdict_reason: Coordination behaviour is real in heavy caregiving, but for weekly check-in calls an explicit ledger is closer to negatively wanted, and the cited evidence documents abandonment rather than demand.
